## Splitting Variables

There are multiple ways to split a variable in R. Now that we know what `$` does, let us look at how to create new columns. To start of, let is create an empty column.

To create an empty column, we will use this command: `Dataframe_name$Name_of_new_column <- NA`. For example:

```{r,echo=F, message=FALSE}
library(readr)
ESS_Subset <- read_csv("~/Downloads/ESS11e04_1-subset (2)/ESS11e04_1-subset.csv")
```

```{r}
ESS_Subset$News_Split <- NA
```

Check the `ESS_Subset` dataframe now! You should have an extra column `News_Split` at the end of the dataframe with all NA Values.

We can also set to this to any value we would like, for example instead of `NA`, we can have all the cells take the value of 0.

```{r}
ESS_Subset$News_Split <- 0
```

::::: {.card .text-white .bg-dark .mb-3 style="max-width: 50rem;"}
::: card-header
Question
:::

::: card-body
<p class="card-text">

What could be a use of first creating an empty column?

</p>

<p class="card-text">

If we are using the `if()` statement in R to create columns, then any row which does not fill the criteria already has some logical value. It also helps with avoiding type conflicts.

</p>
:::
:::::

In today's class, we will look at three ways to split a column variable in R:

:::::::::::::::: {#essExerciseAccordion .accordion}
:::::::: accordion-item
<h2 class="accordion-header" id="stepOne1">

<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseOne1" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseOne1">

Method 1: Using `ifelse()`

</button>

</h2>

::::::: {#collapseOne1 .accordion-collapse .collapse aria-labelledby="stepOne1" data-bs-parent="#essExerciseAccordion"}
:::::: accordion-body
The `ifelse()` function is the quick way to split data. It can get quite messy in many cases. It works by evaluating a logical condition and returning one value if TRUE and another if FALSE. To handle multiple splits, you will have to "nest" the functions.

::::: {.card .text-white .bg-primary .mb-3 style="max-width: 50rem;"}
::: card-header
Tip!
:::

::: card-body
<p class="card-text">

In R, nesting an ifelse() simply means putting a second ifelse() statement inside the "else" (false) slot of the first one.

</p>

The standard syntax for a single `ifelse()` is: `ifelse(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)`

To nest it, you replace value_if_false with a brand new `ifelse()`: `ifelse(condition1, value1, ifelse(condition2, value2, value3))`
:::
:::::

**How can be use this command to split one of our columns?** Give it a try! Try splitting into 2 factors and 3 factors.
::::::
:::::::

<h2 class="accordion-header" id="stepTwo2">

Method 2: Tidyverse with `mutate()` and `case_when()`

</button>

</h2>

::::: {#collapseTwo2 .accordion-collapse .collapse aria-labelledby="stepTwo2" data-bs-parent="#essExerciseAccordion"}
:::: accordion-body
Using tidyverse is cleaner and easy to read. `case_when()` is the cleaner, more powerful version of `ifelse()`. It allows you to list multiple conditions sequentially without nesting!

:::: {#collapseFour4 .accordion-collapse .collapse aria-labelledby="stepFour3" data-bs-parent="#essExerciseAccordion"}
::: accordion-body
The `cut()` function is specifically designed for converting numeric vectors into factors by cutting them into intervals. This is often the best way to split the data which is separated into equal/unequal but consistant intervals.

Based on this, let us attempt the first task for this week:

**Tasks**:

1.  Load the ESS subset from last week

2.  Create a variable for political knowledge or news consumption (`nwspol`) — split into high/low

3.  Compare policy preferences (e.g., redistribution, immigration) between high- and low-information respondents

4.  `ggplot(ess, aes(x = imwbcnt, fill = news_group)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.5)`

**Discussion questions**:

-   Are high- and low-information respondents very different? Or surprisingly similar?

-   If they're similar, what does that imply about shortcuts?

-   If they're different, is information the cause or is something else (education, income) driving both?

## Constructed preferences

**Tasks**:

1.  Find two ESS items that measure "the same thing" differently. For example, immigration measured as economic impact (`imbgeco`) vs. cultural impact (`imueclt`) vs. general ("make country better/worse" `imwbcnt`)

2.  Correlate them: `cor(col1, col2)`

3.  Are they as correlated as you'd expect? Make a scatter plot.

::: {.alert .alert-dismissible .alert-danger}
<button type="button" class="btn-close" data-bs-dismiss="alert">

</button>

<strong>We will do this task together! Let us discuss how to go about this in R!</strong>
:::

**Discussion**:

-   If these all measure "immigration attitudes," why aren't they perfectly correlated?

-   This connects back to Session 2 (Blankenberg, Bosshard): convergent validity failures

-   The way you frame the question shapes the answer
